name: Georgy Malenkov
role: Soviet premier (1953–1955); Second Secretary of the CPSU (1948–1952)
summary: Malenkov was a Stalinist party administrator who ran the cadre apparatus through the purges and, as premier after 1953, argued for more consumer goods, lower peasant taxes and peaceful coexistence while keeping the single-party, planned, collectivised system. His own recorded words are mostly official reports and speeches, so his positions are known mainly on the planned economy, party leadership and Cold War foreign policy.

central-planning.rationale: His report credits the five-year plans with rebuilding and surpassing the pre-war economy and says the socialist economic system will prove its superiority over capitalism.

collective-farming.rationale: The report calls the collective farm system the only form of farming and urges strengthening it; his August 1953 speech again aims at consolidating collective farms.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The report condemns Britain, France, Belgium and the other colonial powers for making their colonies bear the cost of their rearmament and backs the colonial peoples' struggle against imperialist oppression.

defeat-communism.rationale: The report says peaceful coexistence and cooperation of capitalism and communism is fully possible and disclaims any intent to impose the Soviet system by force.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The report holds that the planned socialist economy will prove its superiority over the capitalist one, which is the opposite of the statement.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: The report condemns European states for placing their territory at the disposal of American bases and for giving up an independent national policy, and denounces US bases near Soviet borders.

one-party-rule.rationale: The report says the Soviet order is the best form of social organisation under the Communist Party's leadership and presents the party as the leading force of state, trade unions and youth organisations.

party-controls-media.rationale: The report says the party must control the content of books, newspapers and journals and direct press, propaganda and agitation toward communist education; it speaks of party and state organs rather than 'the government' alone.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: The report demands strict, checked fulfilment of party and government decisions at every level while also calling for inner-party democracy and criticism from below.

patriotic-education.rationale: The report calls on the party to bring up working people in the spirit of Soviet patriotism and friendship between peoples, through all ideological work.

public-ownership.rationale: Malenkov's 19th Congress report presents the socialist (state-owned, planned) economic system as superior to capitalism and calls for strengthening state industry and the state and collective farms.

socialism-one-country.rationale: The report holds that socialism was firmly built in the USSR by its own efforts amid capitalist encirclement, and that the country should strengthen its state; it asks for no revolutions abroad, citing Stalin that exporting revolution is nonsense.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: The report describes the USSR as a socialist society on the way to communism, with a socialist economic system opposed to capitalism.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: The report says a state where socialism has won amid capitalist encirclement must strengthen itself, its army and its punitive and security organs, not weaken, and credits the party with doing so.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Britannica reports that he was deeply involved in the great party purge of the late 1930s, a record of crushing opposition within the party.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The report states that the whole working population of town and country gets free medical care from the state and pledges to expand health care.

vanguard-party.rationale: The report makes the party the leader of the workers and stresses cadres, discipline in carrying out decisions and ideological training.

notes: Searched his 19th Congress report by theme: economy, agriculture, welfare, party and criticism, ideology and media, state, national question, colonies, foreign policy and peace. Only the 1952 report is fully available; the 1953 Supreme Soviet speech is excerpted. His record on purges and the Leningrad affair is reported only in Wikipedia and Britannica, so little of it counts. Most statements on liberty, society, ecology, culture and technology have no recorded position, so the uncertainty rule fails.
